en: [Preface] Having bowed to Mataṅgānana, whose feet are worshipped by the hosts of gods and who, destroying obstacles, generates joy for his devotees,
I shall speak the *Līlāvatī*— a manual of true calculation that bestows delight upon the clever, composed in clear, concise, soft, and pure words, and full of graceful charm.
Twenty cowries (*varāṭaka*) make one *kākiṇī*; four of those make one *paṇa*.
Sixteen of those are understood here as one *dramma*, and likewise, sixteen *drammas* make one *niṣka*.
In this system, a *guñjā* is said to be equal to two barley grains; three *guñjās* make one *valla*, and eight of those make one *dharaṇa*.
Two of those [dharaṇas] make one *gadyāṇaka*; likewise, fourteen *vallas* (equal to fourteen Indra-units) are declared to be one *ghaṭaka*.
Those who know the balance declare that ten half-guñjas make one māṣa; sixteen of those called māṣas make one karṣa;
four karṣas make one pala; and a karṣa of gold is known by the name *suvarṇa*.
Eight barley-corns in thickness constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); four finger-breadths multiplied by six make a cubit (*hasta*).
Four cubits here make a staff (*daṇḍa*), and two thousand of those make a *krośa*.
A *yojana* consists of four *krośas*; likewise, a bamboo staff (*vaṃśa*) consists of ten cubits (*karas*).
A *nivartana* is a field measured by twenty such bamboo staffs and enclosed by four sides.
That which is measured in cubits by its width, length, and depth, having twelve corners, is known as a "solid cubit" (*ghana-hasta*).
That measure of grain and other substances which is one solid cubit in volume is called a *māgadha-khārikā*, as declared in the scriptures.
A *droṇa* is indeed the sixteenth part of a *khārī*; an *āḍhaka* is a quarter of a *droṇa*.
Here, a *prastha* is a fourth part of an *āḍhaka*, and a *kuḍava* is declared by the ancients to be a quarter of a *prastha*.
In this system, a *sera* is said to be equal to two times seven (*14*) *ṭaṅkas*, which are equivalent to one *pāda*-deficient *gadyāṇaka*.
A measure called a *maṇa* consists of four (*20*) *seras*; and in the weighing of grains and the like, it is known by the name *turuṣka*.

The remaining technical definitions, such as those concerning time and so forth, are to be understood as established through common worldly usage. Thus ends the section on technical definitions (paribhāṣā).
[The Eightfold Purification] Now follows the determination of the places of numerical notation.
To him who sports with the black serpent that flickers restlessly from the throat of Līlā—
Homage to Gaṇeśa, whose splendor is as pure as a blue lotus.
[Śloka] One, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a lakh, a prayuta, and a koṭi in succession;
[Gīti] Then an arbuda, an abja, a kharva, a nikharva, a mahāpadma, and from that, a śaṅkha.
The ocean, the end, the middle, and the supreme (parārdha)— these are the names, each ten times greater than the preceding,
established by the ancients for the purpose of conventional usage regarding the places of numbers.
Thus ends the determination of the places of numbers.
Now, addition and subtraction.
Here is the half-verse rule for the procedure of addition and subtraction:
"The sum of the digits, or their difference according to their respective places, should be performed either in direct order or in reverse order."

Now, the method of multiplication:
the rule for multiplication consists of one and a half verses.
(Līlāvatī 14a): One should multiply the last digit of the multiplicand by the multiplier; likewise, one should proceed with the penultimate digit and the others, shifting [the multiplier] each time.
The multiplicand, when multiplied by each of the divisor-segments taken from bottom to top, or when added to the product of those segments,
is divided by that divisor by which the multiplicand is cleared; the quotient thus obtained, when multiplied by the multiplicand, yields the result.
In this way, the division of the form may be twofold: either multiplied separately by the places and then added together,
or multiplied by a multiplier increased or decreased by the desired number, and then either added to or subtracted from the product of the multiplier and the multiplicand.

Alternatively, when the multiplicand is multiplied by the multiplier twenty-eight, and then diminished by eight times the multiplicand, the result is the same: 1,620.
Thus is the method of recitation.
Now, division.
A verse concerning the rule for division:
In division, that multiplier by which the divisor is subtracted from the dividend is indeed the result from the last digit in the division.

Thus ends the section on division by parts.
Now, the section on squares (*varga*).
There are two verses concerning the rule for squaring:

The square of an even number is said to be twice its product with itself. Now, the last term is to be set aside; it is multiplied by twice the last term [and added to the previous result]. *Līlāvatī* 19a.
Likewise, having subtracted other numbers from above their respective places and having removed the last term,
one may take the product of the two parts multiplied by two, added to the sum of the squares of those parts; or else,
the product of the sum and the number diminished by an arbitrary quantity shall be a square, provided it is increased by the square of that arbitrary quantity.

Now, the square root.
A verse on the rule for finding the square root:

Having subtracted the square from the last odd place, double the square root; when that [square] is subtracted from the even place, having subtracted the square of the quotient from the first odd place, set down the quotient multiplied by two.

When the sequence is divided by the sequence, if the quotient is even, subtract one from the odd remainder; divide that by the square of the quotient and place the result in the sequence, doubling it. By repeating this process, the sequence will eventually yield its square root.

[Śārdūlavikrīḍita] Here is the summary: O friend, the square roots of four, nine, and those previously calculated squares— [The verse continues: ...are found by the skillful mathematician. First, one should multiply the last term by the penultimate term, then add the product of the first and third terms; this is the method for finding the square root of a number. One should then divide the result by twice the last term, and from that quotient, subtract the square of the quotient divided by the last term. This process is repeated until the remainder is zero. Thus, the square root is obtained. For example, the square root of 1089 is 33. Furthermore, the square roots of 16, 49, 64, 121, 144, 225, 256, 361, 400, 441, 576, 625, 676, 729, 784, 841, 900, 961, 1024, 1089, 1156, 1225, 1296, 1369, 1444, 1521, 1600, 1681, 1764, 1849, 1936, 2025, 2116, 2209, 2304, 2401, 2500, 2601, 2704, 2809, 2916, 3025, 3136, 3249, 3364, 3481, 3600, 3721, 3844, 3969, 4096, 4225, 4356, 4489, 4624, 4761, 4900, 5041, 5184, 5329, 5476, 5625, 5776, 5929, 6084, 6241, 6400, 6561, 6724, 6889, 7056, 7225, 7396, 7569, 7744, 7921, 8100, 8281, 8464, 8649, 8836, 9025, 9216, 9409, 9604, 9801, 10000, and so forth, are likewise determined. By this method, the square roots of all such numbers are easily found. Thus ends the section on square roots. Now, regarding the calculation of the cube root: one should take the last digit of the number and find its cube root; this is the first digit of the cube root. Then, one should subtract the cube of that digit from the last three digits of the original number and proceed with the remaining digits in the same manner. For example, the cube root of 1728 is 12. Similarly, the cube roots of 2197, 2744, 3375, 4096, 4827, 5615, 6400, 729, 8000, 8748, 9509, and so on, are determined. This concludes the method for extracting cube roots. Now, regarding the calculation of the fourth root (square root of a square root): one should take the last digit of the number and find its square root; this is the first digit of the fourth root. Then, one should subtract the square of that digit from the last two digits of the original number and proceed with the remaining digits in the same manner. For example, the fourth root of 6561 is 9. Similarly, the fourth roots of 8100, 10000, 12100, 14400, 16900, 19600, 22500, 25600, 28900, 32400, 36100, 40000, 44100, 48400, 52900, 57600, 62500, 67600, 72900, 78400, 84100, 90000, 96100, and so forth, are determined. Thus ends the section on fourth roots. Then, one should subtract the fifth power of that digit from the last five digits of the original number and proceed with the remaining digits in the same manner. For example, the fifth root of 32768 is 4. Similarly, the fifth roots of 243, 3125, 1024, 32768, 100000, and so forth, are determined. This concludes the method for extracting fifth roots. Now, regarding the calculation of the sixth root: one should take the last digit of the number and find its sixth root; this is the first digit of the sixth root. Then, one should subtract the sixth power of that digit from the last six digits of the original number and proceed with the remaining digits in the same manner. Thus ends the section on sixth roots. Then, one should subtract the seventh power of that digit from the last seven digits of the original number and proceed with the remaining digits in the same manner. For example, the seventh root of 128 is 2. Know the square-roots of each term individually if an increase in your intellect has arisen here.

Thus ends the section on square roots.
Now, for the cube:
there are three verses on the rule for cubing.
The cube is declared to be the product of three equal quantities. Then, the cube of the last digit is to be set aside, followed by the square of that last digit.

The first term multiplied by three, then the square of the first term multiplied by three times the last term, and finally the cube of the first term—all these, added together with an interval equal to the number of places [between the first term and the last], shall be the cube. Then, having assumed a pair of parts for that, let the last term be determined.
In this way, when the square and the cube are to be established, this procedure should be performed repeatedly starting from the first digit.
Or, a heap multiplied by two parts, tripled, and added to the sum of the cubes of those parts, [results in] the cube of the square root of that heap;
this is the cube of the square-root-heap.
Here is the problem (uddeśaka):

Thus ends the section on the clouds.
Now, two verses concerning the rule for calculation at the root of a cube:
Having subtracted the first cube-place from the next non-cube place, and likewise from each subsequent cube-place starting from the end;
having separately determined the square root of that cube, one should divide the first [remaining] term by three times that square root; the result [is the next digit of the root]. [Upajāti]

One should place the square of that [number] in the row, multiplied by the last [term]; one should subtract three times the cube root of the result from the first term. The cube [of the remainder] is subtracted from the first term, and its cube root is taken; thus the row is formed, and so on again from there.
In this case, for the purpose of finding the roots of the previous cubes, the arrangement is: 729, 19683, 1953125.
The square roots obtained in succession are 9, 27, and 125.
Thus ends the section on the dense root.
